messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marguerite Hollenbeck is a 58-year-old single woman of European descent who currently serves as a city council member in a mid-sized American municipality. She sought psychological consultation after nearly two years of managing, largely in silence, the aftermath of a deployment she undertook as a senior relief coordinator in a conflict zone in Eastern Europe. She had volunteered through an international humanitarian organisation, believing her administrative experience would be useful. What she did not anticipate was arriving during an escalation in shelling, and being present when a supply convoy she had helped organise was struck by an explosion at close range. She was crouched behind a vehicle reviewing a manifest when the blast hit. The sound was not a single bang but a pressure that seemed to collapse the air around her, followed immediately by the laboured, wet breathing of a colleague lying a few feet away — a sound she could not stop and could not help. She has described that breathing as the worst thing she has ever heard: not the explosion itself, but what came after it, the sound of a body trying to continue.

In the months that followed her return, Marguerite found that her memory of the event did not behave as she expected memory to behave. It arrived not as a coherent narrative but as a series of images — the manifest in her hand, the colour of the dust, the angle of light — vivid and discontinuous, as though assembled from photographs taken by someone else. She has described the memory as feeling like it belongs to another person entirely, a dissociative quality that disturbs her almost as much as the content. The memory forces itself into her awareness without invitation, and when it does, it arrives with full sensory force. Hearing heavy breathing — a colleague catching her breath after climbing stairs, a constituent leaning close during a public meeting — is enough to pull her back without warning, and the images flood in with a completeness that the rest of her recollection lacks. Loud bangs on construction sites near city hall, a regular feature of the downtown development her council oversees, have become a particular source of dread; she has reorganised her schedule to avoid walking past active sites, delegating site visits she would previously have handled herself.

The memory, in its fragmented and intrusive form, has steadily reinforced a set of beliefs that Marguerite now holds with quiet conviction. She has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place in a way that feels newly and permanently true — not an abstraction but a fact she carries in her body. This appraisal of pervasive danger sharpens her attentiveness to anything that might signal threat, so that the ordinary sounds of civic life — a car backfiring two blocks from her office, a door slamming in the council chambers — register as potential precursors to something catastrophic, heightening the very vigilance that makes triggers more potent. What frightens her most, however, is the emotional flatness that has settled over her life. She had been a person of considerable warmth and political passion; she now moves through her days with a competence that feels hollow, and she is certain that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. This conviction, that something essential has been permanently lost, makes her reluctant to approach the memory at all. She has come to believe that if she were to sit with it fully, to think about what happened rather than around it, she would not be able to handle it — and so the memory remains unprocessed, its jagged edges unsmoothed, which ensures that when it does intrude, it arrives with undiminished force and confirms, once again, that she was right to fear it.

Marguerite presented for help after she froze at a council meeting when a microphone produced a sharp feedback bang. A colleague noticed. She has described the moment as the first time her private struggle became visible to others, and it alarmed her. She is hoping, cautiously, to recover some of the emotional range she has lost. What she is most afraid of is that the therapy will require her to go somewhere she does not believe she can survive.
